comments.author: @gingerhipster
comments.text:
The funniest thing about nuclear reactors is that all the nuclear energy does is make steam. They're massive futuristic steam turbines. 

TerraPower has a goood innovation in this space: nuclear reactors are dangerous in cases like Chernobyl when the water used to cool the nuclear materials (which generates steam) misbehaves and gets out into the world both violently and gradually, so TerraPower solves this by using pools of molten metal to cover and cool the nuclear materials instead of water. Rather than soaking the rods in water they soak the rods in a metal that absorbs the radiation and also doesn't leak into the ecosystem. The water can be close to this and get hot without getting radioactive. If power is lots the rods stop being charged and gradually cool down inside metal, rather than inside water (which may explode because it's not circulating due to power loss)

There's a bunch of big stuff happening in the next 5 years and we're not ready for it. It's being done to us instead of for us, like everything else, and that's going to cause some serious issues. Don't trust the people who talk about the people but not to the people.

comments.text:
Helion's business model appears, to my eye, to be:

Make slick presentations to investors. Raise billions. Pump the stock. Cash out and disappear.

Are they doing actual science and engineering? Sure. Running experiments? Yep. Showing progress?

Depends on your definition of 'progress.'

See, the breakthrough they need is not getting more power out than they put in.

It's doing it at scale.

No materials can contain a fusion reaction, not even intermittent fusion reactions. It's too hot. So you need magnetic bottles. Immensely strong, stable magnetic bottles. Now how do you get the energy out of the bottle so you can recycle and fuse again? And how fast can you go? And how do you make stable confinement for an intermittent pulse and purge fusion operation?

Hundreds of companies and government labs are working on the problem. None of them will deliver a fusion power plant by 2028. Especially not Helion, whose best expertise appears to be PowerPoint presentations to investors.

Call me skeptical.

Solving the problem of distributed data centers looks trivially easy compared to fusion power plants.

Earth is not a good place to scale up fusion. The sun has plenty going on, however.

Here's what reasoning from first principles gets you, conclusion-wise: moving compute near the sun is more logical than moving the sun close to compute.

You think Elon hasn't thought about this? Mars is his personal obsession, the eggs in basket thing. But the scale he is pursuing. And AI. And robotics. It's obvious that in his mind, there is more than colonization going on. He's going for industrialization of space assets: materials in low-G, ripe for the plucking. And energy. He's moving humanity towards a Kardachev Type II civilization. Compute will mostly happen off-planet, where energy is cheap. Inference in your pocket or vehicle or robot, training in space.

He's working on a long timeline, but that's okay. His vision scales. Best of all, it's cheap. Machines will make machines. Machines will design new machines. We just need cheap launch, and advance the other tech.

Altman is one of those guys blinded by dollar signs in his eyeballs who throws everything at the wall to see if it will stick. It's other people's money. He wants his cut. He is not the guy making breakthroughs. He's the guy promising a bonanza to the real experts. A slick operator. A fast-talking salesman. He's a lubricant, bringing money to the inventive class, guys and gals whose focus is the tech. It has been a fruitful partnership. But don't mistake salesmanship for vision.
